vignette:
He remembers the morning of the accident in pieces-the way the air smelled of wet pine and diesel, the radio playing country on the job site, the sound of a tape measure snapping closed. What he doesn't remember, what he can't keep in his head no matter how many times he tries, is the moment of impact. Just the aftermath: his foreman, Dale, lying on the plywood decking, one arm bent beneath him like a broken wing, the safety harness still clipped to a beam four feet away. The blood coming from Dale's ear was the color of the red clay his grandmother used to dig up in her garden.

That was eight months ago. Now, on his way to work each morning, he drives an extra twelve minutes to avoid the intersection where the ambulance entered the site. He tells his wife, Emily, that traffic is worse on the other route. She doesn't push. He sleeps in the living room recliner most nights because the bed, with its soft mattress and dark corners, feels like a trap. When he does close his eyes, he hears the sliding sound of Dale's boot against the wood, a sound he never actually heard-his brain made it up, he knows, but it plays anyway.

His hands have become a problem. For ten years he's been able to measure, cut, and join wood with the kind of precision that makes other carpenters nod with respect. Now he catches himself staring at a miter saw, waiting for something to go wrong. Twice in the last month he's walked off a job after a loud noise-once when a compressor kicked on, once when an apprentice dropped a framing hammer. The crew has stopped joking about it. His boss, a patient man named Rick, asked him last week if he wanted to take a desk job for a while. He said no. He meant it. But the thought of the drill press starting up again makes his stomach lock like a fist.

Emily has started sleeping in their daughter's room. She doesn't say it, but he knows she's tired of waking up to him thrashing on the couch. Their daughter, Maya, is four. She drew a picture of him last week with big red scribbles over his head. "Daddy's mad," she said. He wasn't mad. He was trying not to flinch at the sound of her spoon scraping the cereal bowl.

He stopped going to the hardware store on Saturdays. Too many people. Too many voices blending into a hum that makes his temples throb. He installed blackout curtains in the garage and now spends his evenings out there, stacking lumber and unstacking it, measuring boards he never cuts. Emily asked him if he wanted to talk to someone. He said no. But he keeps a folded piece of paper in his pocket-the number for the carpenter's union assistance program. He took it from Rick's desk when no one was looking.

Sometimes, when a nail gun fires, he sees Dale's face before the fall, laughing about something. He sees the way the light hit the dust in the air. And then he feels nothing at all, just a hollow space where his chest used to be. He knows something is wrong. He just doesn't know how to lay down the weight he's been carrying.
